name: AI and Authorship
title: AI and Authorship
answer: AI and authorship covers who is credited and who is accountable when artificial intelligence contributes to a research output. It includes text generation, code writing, data analysis, image creation, translation, literature review, and editing, whether the tool is used openly or not. The field asks what counts as a substantive contribution, how AI use is disclosed, and how authorship criteria apply when a system cannot take responsibility. It also touches copyright, plagiarism, peer review confidentiality, and the integrity of the published record. In this site's library, 135 research papers and 13608 extracted claims provide material for tracing how these questions are framed across disciplines.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: AI and authorship covers who is credited and who is accountable when artificial intelligence contributes to a research output. It includes text generation, code writing, data analysis, image creation, translation, literature review, and editing, whether the tool is used openly or not. The field asks what counts as a substantive contribution, how AI use is disclosed, and how authorship criteria apply when a system cannot take responsibility. It also touches copyright, plagiarism, peer review confidentiality, and the integrity of the published record. In this site's library, 135 research papers and 13608 extracted claims provide material for tracing how these questions are framed across disciplines.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on editorial systems, preprint servers, repositories, and peer review platforms that record submissions, versions, reviews, and decisions. It also depends on metadata standards, digital identifiers, disclosure forms, and audit logs that link an output to its authors, institutions, funding, and data. AI writing assistants, code assistants, and image generators are part of the picture because they leave traces that may or may not be captured by those systems. Institutional policies, journal guidelines, and research integrity offices provide the human infrastructure that interprets the records. Provenance tools and plagiarism detection services are used, but their outputs are treated as signals rather than proof.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners compare journal policies, professional guidelines, and institutional rules to see how AI use is defined and disclosed. They review manuscripts, author contribution statements, version histories, and correspondence to test whether credit matches contribution. They may run text analysis, citation checks, image forensics, or provenance audits, and they often interview authors and editors before reaching a finding. Surveys, interviews, and bibliometric studies map how often AI is used and how often it is reported. The method is case based and evidence led, with attention to the limits of detection tools and the possibility of false accusations.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risks center on copyright, licensing, confidentiality, privacy, and the duty to correct the record. Authorship brings accountability, so an AI system cannot be an author if it cannot consent, take responsibility, or face consequences. Provenance is maintained through disclosure statements, contribution records, version control, and metadata that show what was generated, edited, or analyzed with AI. Risks include undisclosed use, fabricated references, plagiarism, breach of peer review confidentiality, biased outputs, and unfair credit allocation. Institutions and publishers handle allegations through their existing misconduct and correction procedures, and they document the evidence and the outcome.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward clearer disclosure norms, better provenance records, and authorship criteria that separate tools from responsible humans. Journals and institutions are likely to keep revising policies as AI systems become more capable and more embedded in writing and analysis. Detection alone is losing favor, and the emphasis is shifting to transparency, audit trails, and reproducible reporting of AI use. Training for researchers, editors, and integrity officers is expanding so that expectations are understood before problems arise. The open questions are how to credit AI assisted work fairly, how to handle generated content in the record, and how to keep public trust in authorship as a signal of responsibility.
